title: Event 7: Swim Standard - Whose Swim Holds Up?
dek: The Day 1 closer is 500 meters of pool swimming broken by 100 burpees, for time. Swimming decided Games leaderboards for a decade before it vanished. Now it is back, and history says it shreds the board.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: Individual Event 7 is Swim Standard: for time, 15-minute cap, a descending swim-and-burpee ladder (200m swim / 40 burpees / 150 / 30 / 100 / 20 / 50 / 10) in a 25-meter pool. It is the first Games swim event since 2022. Our own almanac shows swimming was a Games staple from 2011 to 2019, and the two closest precedents are the 2013 Pool (first 25-yard pool swim) and the 2014 Beach (swim plus burpees, won by Olympic sailing gold medalist Anna Tunnicliffe). Swim events reward a background you either have or you do not, and they produce some of the widest time gaps in the sport.

blocks.text: The official workouts page confirmed the Day 1 closer, and it is the one nobody in this field could fake: **Swim Standard**. For time, under a 15-minute cap: a 200-meter swim, 40 burpees, a 150-meter swim, 30 burpees, a 100-meter swim, 20 burpees, a 50-meter swim, 10 burpees. That is 500 meters of pool swimming, in 25-meter lengths, cut into a descending ladder by 100 total burpees. It streams exclusively on FloElite, and it is the first Games swim event since the 2022 Rinse N Repeat pool intervals.
Why the Swim Is the Great Equalizer

Swimming is the one skill in the sport that does not transfer from land. You can build a huge engine on the rower, the bike and the run and still be genuinely slow in the water, because swim speed lives in technique and comfort, not just fitness. The burpees make it meaner: you climb out of the pool, drop to the deck for a breathless set, then push back off the wall with your heart rate pinned and no ability to control your breathing underwater. Panic is a real factor. The athletes with a swim background will look calm and long in the water while the rest thrash.
The Pool Detail That Matters: 25-Meter Lengths

Five hundred meters in a 25-meter pool is 20 lengths and 19 turns. Every wall is a chance to gain or lose a body length depending on whether you can push off tight and streamlined or come in clumsy and stand up. The ladder is built smart, too: the longest swim (200m) comes first when you are freshest, and both the swims and the burpee sets shrink as the fatigue climbs, so the back half is a test of who can still move when the shoulders are shot.
History First: The Water Has Always Shredded the Board

This is not new territory for the Games, and our almanac makes the pattern obvious. Swimming was a fixture from 2011 through 2019, when the Games opened in the water almost every single year. Two precedents matter most here. The 2013 Pool, at the Woollett Aquatics Center, was the first true pool swim in Games history and it used 25-yard segments, the direct ancestor of this 25-meter pool test. And the 2014 Beach paired swimming with burpees and kettlebell thrusters, the same swim-plus-burpee shape you are watching now.

The winners tell you everything about how these events reward. The 2014 swim event was won on the women side by Anna Tunnicliffe, an Olympic gold medalist, in sailing. A water athlete to her core. Across the whole 2011 to 2019 run, swim mornings routinely produced surprise event winners and buried strength specialists who had no answer once the venue changed from the barbell to the buoy.
What It Means for the Standings

Day 1 has already run the 2007 Hopper, a 7,200-meter trail run, the full CrossFit Total and a bicycle race. Legs and grip are cooked, and the swim rewards a completely different system, which is exactly why it can flip the board. The strength men who owned the Total have no edge in the water. An unheralded swimmer can bank the day of their life. Expect one of the widest time spreads of the weekend: swim events regularly separate the field by a minute or more from top to bottom.
We will post the official podium and the updated overall the moment it scores. History says the name at the top may surprise you.

title: Women's Day 1: Cringle's Takeover, Campbell's Swim, and a Board That Would Not Sit Still
dek: Seven events in one day, and the women's leaderboard changed hands three times before Aimee Cringle ran away with it. How the board actually moved, who did the moving, and who to watch when Day 2 opens.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The women completed all seven Day 1 events. Aimee Cringle ends on top with 458 points and a 38-point cushion after winning three events (the Ranch run, the deadlift and the bike), but she started the day 10th. The lead changed hands from Sturt to Adams to Cringle across the opening events. Lucy Campbell was a metronome at second before demolishing the swim by 69 seconds. Full event-by-event shake-up, the standouts, and the Day 2 watch list - every number verified against the official leaderboard.

blocks.text: Seven scored events in a single day is the most brutal opening the CrossFit Games have ever programmed, and the women's leaderboard treated it like a slalom. The overall lead changed hands three times across the first four events - Sturt, then Adams, then Sturt again, then Cringle - a Swiss rookie cracked the top three in the opening events, and the athlete who ends the day in front - **Aimee Cringle, 458 points** - was sitting **10th** after the very first event. Here is how the board actually moved.
The Takeover: Aimee Cringle

Cringle did not win the opener. She did not even come close: the 2007 Hopper (a 1,000m row into pull-ups and push jerks) left her 10th, and on a normal day that is a hole you spend the weekend digging out of. Instead she won the next thing that mattered and never looked back. She took the **7,200m Ranch run** outright, then the **deadlift** (425 lb), then the **bike race** - three event wins in three completely different domains. Endurance, max strength, and a leg-burning time trial, all won by the same 27-year-old from the Isle of Man who finished 8th here a year ago. She took the overall lead after the shoulder press and pushed it to a 38-point gap by nightfall. That is not a hot streak. That is range.
The Shake-Up, Event by Event
This is the part that makes a Day 1 fun, so let us walk the board the way it actually happened.

**After Event 1 (Hopper):** Madeline Sturt on top, winning the opener in 8:03. Lucy Campbell 2nd, Swiss rookie Aline Wirz a stunning 3rd. Cringle 10th, Alex Gazan 12th - the strength athletes buried, the engines up front.

**After Event 2 (Ranch 7200):** the run flipped it. Cringle won it in 40:42 with Haley Adams right behind (41:15), and Adams' Hopper-plus-run combination briefly put the **veteran into the overall lead**. Cringle surged to 5th. This was still anyone's day.

**Through the CrossFit Total (Events 3-5):** the strength block scrambled everything, twice. Quarterfinals winner **Kyra Milligan stole the back squat at 370 lb**, which nudged Sturt back into the overall lead. Then the shoulder press turned it over again: **Gazan won it at 170**, Sturt could only manage 27th, and Cringle inherited the lead she would not surrender. She slammed the door by winning the **deadlift at 425** to close the Total. When the barbell was loaded away, Cringle was 1st overall and the specialists had made their mark and slid back down.

**After Event 6 (Bike):** Cringle again, 19:10, her third win - and one of the closest finishes of the day behind her, with Emma Lawson (19:17.29) edging Campbell (19:17.30) for second by one hundredth of a second.
**After Event 7 (Swim):** Campbell's turn, and it was not close. More on that below.
Who Did Well

**Lucy Campbell (2nd, 420)** was the most consistent athlete on the floor. Read her overall rank through the day: 2nd, 2nd, 2nd, 2nd, then 4th, 3rd, 2nd. A metronome. The 2025 Games runner-up and reigning Open champion never had the single best event until the water, and then she had the best event by a mile. She is 38 points back and has the most complete resume in the chase.

**Madeline Sturt (3rd, 407)** won the opener and led early; the Australian engine and gymnastics are real. She faded only where you would expect, giving back ground in the swim (9th), but a podium spot after Day 1 continues a career-best arc for an athlete who was out of the Games entirely from 2020 to 2023.

**Haley Adams (4th, 372)** wore the overall lead for a moment after the run and stayed glued to the top five all day. The 2018 Fittest Teen keeps compounding a comeback most people did not expect after her 2023 step-away.

**Emma Lawson (5th, 364)** did the quiet thing that wins weekends: she climbed. Seventh, seventh, seventh, then a steady grind up to fifth by the swim. The youngest woman ever to podium at the Games (2nd in 2023 at age 18) sat out all of 2025 with a back injury. She looks healthy, and healthy Lawson is a problem for everyone above her.

**Alex Gazan (6th, 325)** is the wildcard. She won the shoulder press, took second on the deadlift, and owns one of the heaviest barbells in the field - then the bike (25th) reminded everyone why the Total is only three of twenty events. If Day 2 goes heavy, she is dangerous.
The Swim Was the Great Equalizer, Exactly As Promised

**We said before Event 7** that swimming is the one skill that does not transfer from land fitness, and that it reliably shreds a CrossFit leaderboard. It did. **Campbell won the Swim Standard in 10:55 - 69 seconds clear of the field** (Paige Rodgers 12:04, Danielle Brandon 12:18). That is not a CrossFitter who swims. That is a **former international swimmer** doing her actual sport, and the gap showed it. It cut the other way for the non-swimmers: Adams took 8th in the water, Sturt 9th, Wirz 14th, each bleeding points they had banked on the barbell and the run. Preparation meets the pool, and the pool does not care about your back squat.
People to Watch on Day 2

**Cringle** leads, but a 38-point cushion after 7 of 20 events is a headline, not a trophy. Her range is the real reason to believe: an athlete who can win a 7km run and a max deadlift on the same day does not have an obvious hole to attack.

**Campbell** is the hunter. Nearly the same points profile as the leader, and the deepest big-stage resume in the group. If the arena days bring classic barbell-and-gymnastics couplets, expect her to close.

**The 4-through-8 cluster is tight** - Adams (372) down to Arielle Loewen (300) is separated by a single strong event. Loewen, a 2023 podium finisher, already clawed from 16th back to 8th on the strength of a 4th-place swim. That group will reorder fast.

**And keep an eye on the rookie.** Aline Wirz, 32, sits 7th after being diagnosed with a C6 neck fracture roughly five weeks before her semifinal. Seventh at the CrossFit Games after Day 1, on that backstory, is one of the quiet stories of the weekend.
Seven events down, thirteen to go. The board churned this much in one day - so hold your final takes. The men's Day 1 recap is next, and their swim has not even scored yet.

title: Men's Day 1: Jay Crouch Led Wire to Wire, Then the Water Took It
dek: The same story as the women, told louder. Jay Crouch led after every one of the first six events, the swim knocked him to fourth, and James Sprague inherited the lead. How the men's board moved, and who is still alive with thirteen events to go.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The men finished all seven Day 1 events. Jay Crouch led the overall after every event from the Hopper through the bike, then a 19th-place swim dropped him to 4th on the final event of the day. James Sprague (the 2024 champion) took over the lead at 418 (officials later revised some Day 1 scores), ahead of Dallin Pepper (413), with two-time champion Justin Medeiros 3rd. Ty Jenkins won the swim, Colten Mertens swept the Total's squat and press, and the reigning champion Jayson Hopper sits 8th. Top five separated by 28 points. Every number verified against the official leaderboard.

blocks.text: If you want the shape of the men's Day 1 in one sentence: Jay Crouch led after every single event from the opener through the bike, and then he went swimming. The Australian sat first overall for six straight events - a wire-to-wire day in the making - until the Swim Standard caught him, dropped him to 19th on the event, and knocked him to **4th overall** on the last test of the night. Behind him, **James Sprague inherited the lead.** Here is how the board moved.
Wire to Wire, Then the Water

Crouch was magnificent for most of the day. He won the 2007 Hopper outright in 7:11, took 3rd on the Ranch run, and did the quietly harder thing through the strength block - he never won a lift, but he never bled enough points to lose the lead either. Six events, six times atop the overall board. Then the pool did what the pool does. A 19th-place swim is a small crack on most days; on the final event of a seven-event marathon, with the field this tight, it cost him three spots and the lead. He is 4th, 27 points off the top, and he still had one of the best days on the floor. That is how brutal this opening was.
The Shake-Up, Event by Event
**After Event 1 (Hopper):** Crouch on top, winning the opener in 7:11. Colten Mertens 2nd, Saxon Panchik 3rd. Dallin Pepper, who ends the day 2nd overall, opened in 17th.
**After Event 2 (Ranch 7200):** Ricky Garard won the 7,200m run in 39:33, with Sprague 2nd (39:43) and Crouch 3rd (39:52) - three men inside 20 seconds after 4.5 miles. Crouch held the overall lead.

**Through the CrossFit Total (Events 3-5):** the strength kings had their moment. **Mertens swept the first two lifts** - a 555 lb back squat and a 260 lb shoulder press - and **Patrick Vellner won the deadlift at 605 lb** at age 36. Crouch, no one's idea of a strength specialist, simply refused to fall apart (14th squat, 11th press, 18th deadlift) and carried his lead straight through the barbell.

**After Event 6 (Bike):** a photo finish - Moritz Fiebig won the Grass Oval by 0.14 of a second over Pepper, with the top five inside three-quarters of a second. Crouch was 3rd and, yes, still led overall.
**After Event 7 (Swim):** the day flipped. More below.
Who Did Well

**James Sprague (1st, 414)** did what champions do: he was never worse than good and he was there at the end. The 2024 Fittest Man on Earth ground out a 2nd on the run, a 2nd on the deadlift and a top-six swim, and when Crouch cracked, Sprague was the one standing in front. He leads Day 1 by five points after the officials' revised scoring (418 to Pepper's 413).

**Dallin Pepper (2nd, 413)** authored the best climb of the day. Seventeenth after the Hopper, then 9th, 10th, 8th, 6th, 4th, and finally 2nd - a relentless march up the board capped by a 3rd-place swim. The 2024 runner-up and three-time teen world champion is one point off the lead and trending the right way.

**Justin Medeiros (3rd, 392)** reminded everyone the two-time champion does not have obvious holes. He sat mid-pack early, took 2nd in the swim, and slid into the final podium spot. Quiet, efficient, dangerous.

**Ricky Garard (5th, 386)** won the run and never left the top five. The 2025 runner-up, four years removed from a doping ban he came back to erase, keeps stacking consistent finishes - exactly the profile that wins long weekends.

**And the strength men made their statement:** Mertens took two event wins in the Total and Vellner took a third; both will be salivating if Day 2 brings heavy barbell. Mertens sits 9th only because the bike (0 points) and the swim buried an otherwise huge day.
The Swim Was the Great Equalizer, Again

Same lesson the women taught a few hours earlier. **Ty Jenkins - a former three-time teen world champion and one of the youngest men in the field - won the Swim Standard outright in 11:09**, ahead of Medeiros (11:23) and Pepper (11:49). And it cut the legs out from under the leader: Crouch's 19th in the water is the single reason Sprague is wearing the overall lead tonight instead of him. The pool does not care who led on the barbell.
People to Watch on Day 2

**The whole top five is live.** Sprague (418), Pepper (413), Medeiros (388), Crouch (387) and Garard (386) are packed into 32 points. One event reorders all of them. This is not a race with a runaway - it is a knife fight.

**Where is the champ?** Reigning Fittest Man on Earth Jayson Hopper sits 8th (304). He had no bye and had to requalify the hard way after a groin injury, and Day 1 was clearly a grind for him. But defending champions do not usually stay 8th - watch whether he climbs when the arena events start.

**And watch Crouch's response.** Leading wire to wire and losing it on the last event of the day can break an athlete or light a fire. He has the engine and the gymnastics for the arena. How he answers Day 2 will tell us whether Day 1 was a fluke of one bad discipline or a real ceiling.

Seven down, thirteen to go, three former champions in the top eight and none of them running away. Hold your final takes - the men's board proved today it can turn over on a single event. The end-of-day data breakdown is next.

title: The Rookie Report: How the 15 First-Timers Handled Day 1
dek: Six men, nine women, zero Games experience between them, and a seven-event opener that would rattle a veteran. Three of them still walked off an event podium. Here is how every 2026 rookie handled Day 1.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The 2026 field has 15 Games rookies (6 men, 9 women). On a brutal seven-event opening day, three of them reached an event podium: Aline Wirz (3rd, Hopper), Ella Wilkinson (3rd, Ranch 7200) and Dylan Hamming (3rd, shoulder press). Wirz sits 7th overall, the only rookie in the top 10, on the back of an elite engine and despite a rough CrossFit Total. The class also skews young (Miley Wade is 18, the youngest in the field) and it was not spared by the day - Hannah Black fought ankle trouble on the run. Every number verified against the official leaderboard.

blocks.text: Fifteen athletes walked into the 2026 CrossFit Games with zero individual Games experience - six men, nine women - and the sport did not ease them in. Seven scored events in a single day is the most brutal opener ever programmed, the kind of day that rattles athletes who have done this for a decade. And yet three of these first-timers walked off an event podium. Here is how the whole rookie class handled Day 1.
Three Rookies, Three Podiums

Start with the headline. **Aline Wirz took 3rd in the opening Hopper** (8:16), behind only Madeline Sturt and Lucy Campbell. **Ella Wilkinson ran to 3rd in the Ranch 7200** (42:16), a 7,200-meter trail race, beaten only by Aimee Cringle and Haley Adams. And on the men side, **Dylan Hamming pressed 245 lb for 3rd in the shoulder press**, one rung below Colten Mertens and Ricky Garard. Three rookies who did not merely survive an event - they beat almost every veteran in it.
The Rookie of Day 1: Aline Wirz

Switzerland's Wirz, 32, sits **7th overall** after Day 1, the only rookie in either division inside the top 10. Her card tells you exactly who she is: 3rd on the Hopper, 4th on the bike, an engine that belongs at this level. The CrossFit Total exposed the gap - 27th, 29th and 29th on the three lifts - but she had banked so much on the mono-structural events that she held a top-seven spot through the barbell block anyway. And remember the backstory: she was diagnosed with a C6 neck fracture roughly five weeks before her semifinal. Seventh at the CrossFit Games after Day 1, on that timeline, is the story of this rookie class.
The Young Guns

Three of these rookies are barely out of the teen ranks. **Miley Wade, at 18 the youngest athlete in the entire field**, took 8th on the Ranch run and sits 25th - completely at home. **Iceland's Bergros Bjornsdottir, 19**, was the steadiest rookie on the floor: a best of 8th on the back squat and nothing worse than 24th across all seven events, good for 15th overall on debut. And **Chile's Benjamin Reyes, 21**, had the hardest day of the group, but he made it here, and he is 21. This class has a future.
The Men's Class

Georgia's **Nika Maisuradze** led the rookie men in 17th, with a pair of 6th-place finishes - the Ranch run and the deadlift - that point to a real all-around base. Spain's **Luis Cuellar**, 19th, saved his best for last with a 5th in the Swim Standard, a rookie who can actually swim in a field where most cannot. And **Dylan Hamming**, at 33 the oldest rookie in the field, announced himself on the barbell with that 3rd-place press. Different ages, different tools, same result: they belonged.
Day 1 Also Took a Toll

The opener was punishing, and not everyone came through it clean. Per BoxRox's Day 1 coverage, Anika Greer competed on an injured ankle. (BoxRox also listed Henrik Haapalainen as racing on an Achilles injury - Henrik has since set the record straight himself: the injury was about 20 months ago, he has fully recovered, and he is not racing hurt.) Among the rookies, **Hannah Black dealt with ankle trouble on the same trail run** and did not post a scored result on the bike. The steep Ranch climbs forced multiple athletes to walk sections of the course. Day 1 was a test of durability as much as fitness, and the newcomers felt every bit of it.
What Day 2 Holds

The arena events (8 through 12) reward a different toolkit than Day 1's strength-and-engine poles: high-skill gymnastics, barbell cycling, mixed triplets under fatigue. That is neutral-to-good news for the rookies who lost ground on the Total, like Wirz and Wilkinson, and a real test for the ones who leaned on it. First-timers carry no scar tissue from a bad Games day and none of the pressure of defending a ranking. Watch whether Wirz can hold the top 10 when the barbell gets technical - and whether one of these names sneaks another event podium indoors.
Fifteen first-timers walked into the deepest field the sport has ever assembled, and three of them left Day 1 standing on an event podium. Whatever Friday brings, this class arrived.

title: The Champions Check-In: Where the Last Four Winners (and Every Podium Vet) Stand
dek: For the first time in the modern era, the last four men to win the CrossFit Games are all on the same floor. Day 1 scattered them from 1st to 11th. Here is where every former champion and podium finisher sits, and what the remaining tests hold for each of them.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The 2026 field contains the last four men's champions - Justin Medeiros (2021, 2022), Jeffrey Adler (2023), James Sprague (2024) and Jayson Hopper (2025) - plus eight more athletes with a Games podium. After Day 1: Sprague leads at 418, Medeiros is 3rd, Hopper 8th, Adler 11th. The podium vets: Pepper 2nd, Garard 5th, Khrennikov 7th, Vellner 22nd but with an event win. On the women's side there is no former champion in the field at all - the 2026 winner will be a first-time champion - and podium vets Campbell (2nd), Lawson (5th) and Loewen (8th) are all in the hunt. Grounded reads on who fits the remaining announced tests. All numbers from the official leaderboard, including the officials' revised Day 1 scoring.

blocks.text: Here is a fact that has never been true in the modern era of this sport: **the last four men to win the CrossFit Games are all competing on the same floor this weekend.** Justin Medeiros (2021 and 2022), Jeffrey Adler (2023), James Sprague (2024) and Jayson Hopper (2025). Four champions, four completely different Day 1 stories - one leads the Games, one is buried in 11th. And behind them stand eight more athletes who have touched a Games podium. This is the deepest collection of proven winners the Games have ever assembled, so let us check in on every one of them. A quick note on the numbers: officials revised some Day 1 scores after the initial postings, and everything below reflects the current official leaderboard.
The Four Champions

**James Sprague, 2024 champion - 1st overall, 418 points.** The 24-year-old is doing exactly what won him the title: never being bad at anything. Second on the Ranch run, second on the deadlift, top six in the swim, and when Jay Crouch cracked in the water, Sprague was the one standing there. His worst event was the shoulder press (26th), and he still leads the Games. That is a champion's scorecard.

**Justin Medeiros, 2021 and 2022 champion - 3rd overall, 388 points.** The only two-time winner in the field is quietly assembling a classic Medeiros weekend: no event outside the top 13 except the press, a 2nd-place swim to close the day, and a profile with almost no holes. He has been here before - twice - and the arena, where he built both titles, opens Friday.

**Jayson Hopper, 2025 champion - 8th overall, 304 points.** The reigning champ had the grinding day of the four: nothing better than 5th (the bike), an 18th on the run, and a field that gave him nothing for free. But 8th after the most brutal opening day ever programmed is not a crisis, it is a starting position. He had to requalify the hard way this season after a groin injury, and he has already shown he can win a Games from inside the pack.

**Jeffrey Adler, 2023 champion - 11th overall, 281 points.** The Canadian's day peaked early with a 4th on the Ranch run and an 8th in the swim, but the strength block (19th, 21st, 19th) and the bike (25th) bled points. Eleventh is the deepest hole of the four champions - and worth remembering: Adler won his title in 2023 as a grinder who stacked the back half of the weekend.
The Podium Chasers - Men

**Dallin Pepper (2nd in 2024) - 2nd overall, 413.** The best climb of Day 1: 17th after the Hopper, 2nd by nightfall, capped with podium finishes on the bike and in the swim. The three-time teen world champion has been runner-up once and is positioned to go one better.

**Ricky Garard (2nd in 2025) - 5th overall, 386.** Won the Ranch 7200 outright and took 2nd in the press - the rare athlete scoring at both poles of the day. The squat (26th) is the outlier on the card. Five points off the podium with thirteen events left.

**Roman Khrennikov (2nd in 2022) - 7th overall, 341.** Steady more than spectacular: 4th on the press, top seven on the bike and in the swim. And the test he may be waiting for is already published - more on that below.

**Patrick Vellner (2nd in 2018, five career podiums) - 22nd overall, 180.** The hardest card of the group, with one shining exception: at 36, Vellner **won the deadlift at 605 lb**, beating every young gun in the field. The official board shows no scored result for him in the swim, which is a major reason for the position. Whatever the weekend holds, that deadlift was a statement.
The Women: A New Champion Is Guaranteed

Here is the quiet headline of the women's race: **there is no former champion in the 2026 women's field.** Whoever wins on Sunday becomes a first-time Fittest Woman on Earth. The athletes with podium pedigree chasing that open crown:

**Lucy Campbell (2nd in 2025) - 2nd overall, 420.** The most credentialed woman in the field is running the same race as last year, one step off the lead. Her Day 1: top four in four events (2nd on the Hopper, 4th on the Ranch run, 3rd on the bike, 1st in the swim) and a 69-second demolition of that swim. She has also now won both of the last two Games pool-swim events (2022 and 2026).

**Emma Lawson (2nd in 2023) - 5th overall, 364.** Back from a year lost to injury and climbing all day: 2nd on the bike, 5th in the swim, and the youngest woman ever to podium at the Games (2nd in 2023 at age 18) is 21 years old now, with room to move.

**Arielle Loewen (3rd in 2023) - 8th overall, 300.** Recovered from a slow start (21st on the run) with a 4th-place swim. The 2023 podium finisher self-coaches from a garage gym in Texas and keeps beating athletes with entire support teams.

**Olivia Kerstetter (3rd in 2025) - 17th overall, 220.** The toughest Day 1 of the podium group, though the strength block showed her tools: 9th on the squat, 4th on the deadlift. If the arena goes heavy, she climbs.
Who Fits What Is Left

Four of the remaining tests are already published, and our almanac gives several of these veterans a verified history with them. **The 500m sprint (Event 13)** - Ricky Garard won both parts of 2024 Track and Field, the closest thing to a sprint credential a Games athlete can hold. **Machine 7200m (row 3,600 + ski 3,600, Sunday)** - Roman Khrennikov won BOTH of its nearest ancestors, the 2020 1,000m row and the 2022 Rinse N Repeat machine interval, and Lucy Campbell won that 2022 event on the women's side. **Roll to Support (the ring AMRAP, Sunday)** - Patrick Vellner is a former artistic gymnast who competed on apparatus into 2010, the cleanest rings technician in the field. **The Speed Snatch Triple (Event 15)** is a rerun of the 2020 test, and the field's proven 1RM snatcher, Guilherme Malheiros (won the 2021 max snatch at 305 lb), is the threat to everyone here.

And the unannounced arena events (8 through 12) reward exactly what champions are made of: high-skill gymnastics and barbell under fatigue, in front of a crowd. Medeiros built two titles in that environment. Sprague won his there last year. Hopper won his there four months after that. The engine specialists owned Day 1. The arena belongs to the winners.

Thirteen events left. Four men who know exactly what winning this thing takes, a women's crown that is guaranteed to change hands, and every podium vet within striking distance of something. This is the weekend the resumes start to matter.

title: 3D Throw: The Games Have Not Thrown Anything Since 2012. Whose Power Flies?
dek: Friday opens with three throws for total distance - right, left, backward - at 30 lb for the men and 20 for the women. Throwing has not been tested at the Games in 14 years, and the last time it was, the board got scrambled. Here is who the physics favors.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The official workouts page published the 3D Throw for Friday, July 24: for total distance, one throw right, one throw left, one throw backward (30 lb men / 20 lb women, presented by Rogue; implement type and event number not yet announced). Our almanac shows throwing for distance has appeared only twice at the Games - the 2011 softball throw (inside a combined skills event) and the 2012 GHD Ball Toss, a backward toss for distance at just 4 and 2 lb. At 30 and 20 lb this is a different animal: body mass times total-body power. The grounded reads: Hopper (100 kg, ex-college wide receiver), Khrennikov (103 kg, the heaviest man in the field), Hamming (98 kg and 3rd in the press), Maisuradze (ex-football running back) for the men; Hannah Black (82 kg, the heaviest woman, top-10 in all three Total lifts), Kerstetter and Gazan for the women. With one big caveat: throws are a skill CrossFitters do not train, and novelty events reliably produce surprises.

blocks.text: The official workouts page just published Friday's opener, and it is the most unusual test of the weekend so far. The **3D Throw**: for total distance, **one throw to the right, one throw to the left, and one throw backward**. Men throw 30 lb, women 20 lb. Presented by Rogue. That is the entire published prescription - the implement type and the individual event number are not yet announced, and we will not guess either.
The Games Have Not Thrown Anything in 14 Years

Search our almanac for throwing events and you find exactly two, both from the sport's early era. The **2011 softball throw** - max distance, two attempts - lived inside a combined skills event alongside an L-sit and a handstand walk. And the **2012 Ball Toss**: athletes sat in a GHD and threw medicine balls overhead, backward, for distance. That 2012 event is the direct ancestor of Friday's backward throw - and it was contested with **4 lb balls for the men and 2 lb for the women**. Friday's implements are more than seven times heavier. This is not a touch-and-accuracy test. It is a power test wearing a skill test's clothes.

Worth remembering what happened in 2012: the Ball Toss was won by **Chad Mackay and Cheryl Brost** - not the era's dominant names. Novelty tests scramble boards. Neither 2012 winner is in this field, so nobody here has thrown for Games points before. Every athlete starts from zero.
The Physics: Mass Times Power, Three Directions

Throwing a heavy implement for distance rewards two things above all: **body mass and total-body power** - the same recipe as the shot put. The rotational throws (right and left) add a wrinkle: they demand hip-and-torso rotation in BOTH directions, and almost nobody trains rotational power symmetrically. The backward throw is the purest expression: hips, legs, and back launching the load overhead - mechanically a cousin of yesterday's deadlift. Total distance across all three means consistency beats one monster heave: you cannot hide a weak side.
The Grounded Reads: Men

**Jayson Hopper** is the read the data likes most: at **100 kg he is the second-heaviest man in the field**, and he is an **ex-college wide receiver** - the one athlete here whose sporting DNA is literally a ball in flight. Sitting 8th overall, the reigning champ could use exactly this kind of Friday opener. **Roman Khrennikov (103 kg)** is the heaviest man here and took 4th in the press. **Dylan Hamming (98 kg, 3rd in the shoulder press at 245 lb)** has the best mass-plus-pressing-power combination among the rookies. **Nika Maisuradze** is a former American-football running back. And **Colten Mertens** - who won both the squat and the press yesterday - has the most event-verified power in the field, though at 86 kg he gives up mass to the big men.
The Grounded Reads: Women

**Hannah Black** is the sneaky pick: at **82 kg she is the heaviest woman in the field by a full 7 kg**, and she went top-10 in all three lifts of the Total (6th squat, 9th press, 10th deadlift). Sitting 29th after a rough Day 1 with ankle trouble, she has every incentive to empty the tank on a test built for her frame. **Olivia Kerstetter (73 kg, 4th in the deadlift, 9th in the squat)** has the power profile. **Alex Gazan won the shoulder press outright** and set the women's Total record - the pressing power is real, though at 68 kg she gives up mass. And watch **Lucy Campbell (73 kg)**: no specific throwing credential, but the total-body power that won the swim travels.
The Caveat That Matters

Throwing is a technique sport. Shot-putters spend years on footwork, angle of release, and timing - none of which this field trains. With the event published roughly a day before it is contested, nobody is building a throw overnight. Expect technique to compress the gaps the physics predicts, and expect at least one name nobody picked to launch one. That is what the 2012 toss did, and it is half the fun. A model read, not a result prediction.

Friday opens the arena days. The 3D Throw starts them with something the sport has not asked in 14 years: how far can you throw it? We will have the podium and the updated board the moment it is official.

title: Day 2 Is Loaded: The Snail Returns, a Handstand Sprint, Heavy Hang Cleans and That Throw
dek: Four of Friday's five arena-day events are now published, and our almanac has history on three of them. The Snail is back after a decade, the Handstand Sprint name is straight from 2020, and one woman in this field has won three handstand-walk events in a row.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The official workouts page published three more Friday events alongside the 3D Throw: Climbing Snail 26 (400-lb Snail pushes, legless rope climbs, 30 toes-to-bars, rope climbs, in weight vests, 10-min cap), Run Hang Squat Clean (4 rounds of 660m run + 10 hang squat cleans at 225/155 on a short barbell), and Handstand Sprint (a handstand walk course, 6-min cap). History first: the 2016 Climbing Snail was won by Fikowski and Briggs; the 2020 Handstand Sprint by Fraser and Wells; and in the current field, Danielle Brandon has won three handstand-walk-family events (2021-2023), Nick Mathew won the 2022 Skill Speed Medley, and Crouch and Campbell won the 2025 run-barbell-handstand Grip Trip. One Friday event remains unannounced.

blocks.text: The workouts page just went from quiet to loaded. Alongside the 3D Throw, CrossFit published three more Friday events, which means **four of the five arena-day tests are now public** (one remains unannounced, likely a FloElite exclusive). Here is each one, with the history our almanac has on it.
Climbing Snail 26: The Snail Is Back After a Decade

For time, 10-minute cap: a **400-lb Snail push** (100 feet for the men, 60 for the women), legless rope climbs (3 men / 2 women), **30 toes-to-bars**, rope climbs (5 men / 4 women), and a closing Snail push - all of it wearing a **weight vest** (22 lb men / 16 lb women). The name is a direct callback: the **2016 Climbing Snail** paired berm runs, rope ascents and Snail pushes, and it was won by **Brent Fikowski and Samantha Briggs**. Neither is in this field, so the title is open. The demands are brutal grip and midline under load: legless climbs after pushing a 400-lb implement, then holding a rig with a vest dragging on you. Grip survivors win it.
Handstand Sprint: One Athlete Owns This History

For time, a handstand walk course under a 6-minute cap. The name comes straight from the **2020 Handstand Sprint** - a 100-yard walk at the Ranch won by Mat Fraser (1:20.85) and Brooke Wells (1:21.22). And this is where our almanac gets loud, because handstand-walk events are a Games staple and the current field has serious receipts. **Danielle Brandon has won three straight handstand-walk-family events: the 2021 Handstand Walk Obstacle Course, the 2022 Skill Speed Medley, and the 2023 Inverted Medley.** Nobody in the sport owns this movement family like she does, and after a quiet Day 1 (13th), this is her springboard. On the men's side, **Nick Mathew won that same 2022 Skill Speed Medley**, and **Jay Crouch and Lucy Campbell both won the 2025 Albany Grip Trip**, which closed four of five rounds with a 100-foot handstand walk (150 feet in the final round). Saxon and Spencer Panchik also carry family pedigree here - their brother Scott won the 2021 obstacle course.
Run Hang Squat Clean: No Precedent, Pure Engine-Barbell

4 rounds for time: **660-meter run, 10 hang squat cleans at 225 lb men / 155 lb women on a short barbell**. Our almanac finds no exact precedent for a run-plus-hang-squat-clean interval, which makes this the most honest test of Friday: run fast with heavy legs, then cycle a heavy barbell with a spiked heart rate, four times. The profile it rewards - engine plus heavy barbell under fatigue - reads like the athletes who scored at both poles of Day 1: Garard (won the run, 2nd in the press), Sprague (2nd run, 2nd deadlift), and on the women's side Cringle (won the run AND the deadlift) and Sturt. The short barbell is a wrinkle: less whip, less forgiveness, more precision when tired.
Plus the Throw, and One Mystery Left

The **3D Throw** (three throws for total distance, 30/20 lb) has its own full breakdown on the site - the first Games throwing test since 2012, and a body-mass-times-power lottery with a technique twist. That makes four of five Friday events public. The fifth remains unannounced; based on the broadcast schedule, expect it to surface on FloElite. We will cover it the moment it is official - no guessing before then.
What Friday Means for the Board

Day 1 tested the poles: maximal strength and raw engine. Friday is the middle we said was coming - gymnastics skill (handstand course, rope climbs, toes-to-bars), odd objects under load, and barbell-engine blends. The leaders who got there on engine alone now have to hold on through skill; the gymnasts buried by the Total get their events at last. With the top five men separated by 32 points and Cringle's cushion at 38, Friday is where the 2026 Games actually take shape. Cards and boards the moment each event is official.

title: The Hopper Draw Returns: Friday Ends With a Workout Nobody Has Seen
dek: On Friday morning, the original 2007 hopper drum gets spun live at Opening Ceremonies. Whatever comes out gets contested by the individual field that same night. This is the sport's founding idea - unknown and unknowable - made into an event, and it is the purest test of the whole weekend.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: CrossFit confirmed the hopper draw returns at the 2026 Games: on the morning of Friday, July 24, during Opening Ceremonies, a workout is drawn live from the ORIGINAL 2007 hopper drum in front of athletes and fans, and the individual field competes the drawn test that same Friday night (reported as the night-session closer, expected to be Event 12; the official number is pending). The 2007 draw produced the 1,000m row + pull-ups + push jerks test that opened these very Games as Event 1. A hopper rewards the athlete with no holes: nobody can prepare, everybody finds out together. Who the no-holes read favors, grounded in Day 1 spreads and our capacity data.

blocks.text: Here is the most CrossFit thing that will happen all weekend. On **Friday morning, during Opening Ceremonies**, CrossFit will spin the **original hopper drum from the 2007 Games** - the actual barrel - live in front of the athletes and the crowd, and draw a workout out of it. Whatever comes out, the individual field competes it **that same Friday night**. Per the announcement, the drawn test combines two modalities; the official event number is still pending (by the broadcast schedule it closes Friday as Event 12). No preview. No pacing plan. Nobody has seen it, because it does not exist yet.
The Origin Myth, Full Circle Twice

The hopper is not a gimmick, it is the founding document. In 2007, at the first Games on a ranch in Aromas, the field learned their test when it came out of a barrel: a 1,000-meter row, then 5 rounds of 25 pull-ups and 7 push jerks. That draw became one of the most iconic workouts in the sport - iconic enough that **these very Games opened with it on Wednesday as Event 1**, where Jay Crouch (7:11) and Madeline Sturt (8:03) nearly halved the 2007 winning times. And now the same physical drum that created that workout gets spun again to create a new one. The 2026 Games opened with the last hopper's answer and will run its next question two days later.
Why This Is the Purest Test

CrossFit's definition of fitness was built on exactly this: **preparedness for the unknown and unknowable**. Every other event this weekend was announced, studied, and strategized. This one cannot be. A hopper strips away coaching, pacing scripts and specialist prep, and asks the only question the sport was founded on: are you fit for whatever comes out? Our whole analytical model - the hopper quadrant in the Capacity Lab, the Hopper Readiness index on our daily WOD tracker - is built on this idea, and on Friday night it stops being a model and becomes an event.
Who a Hopper Favors: The No-Holes Athletes

You cannot prepare for a hopper, but you can BE prepared for it, and Day 1 already told us who that is. A hopper punishes the athlete with one great weapon and rewards the athlete with no bad ones. On the men's side, that reads like **James Sprague** - outside the two strength lifts, the leader never finished worse than 6th on Day 1 - and **Dallin Pepper**, who climbed to 2nd without winning anything, the classic no-holes scorecard. **Justin Medeiros** built two titles on exactly this profile. On the women's side, **Aimee Cringle just won events in three different domains in one day** (a trail run, a max deadlift, a bike race) - it is hard to imagine a better hopper resume - and **Lucy Campbell** was top four in four of seven events. The athletes who should be nervous are the specialists who bank on knowing what is coming.

One more layer: fatigue. The drawn workout runs at the END of Friday night, after the Snail, the throws, the hang cleans and the handstand course. Whatever comes out of the barrel lands on a field that has already been through four events that day. The unknown, on empty tanks, under arena lights. That is as honest as this sport gets.

We will publish the drawn workout the moment it is official on Friday morning, with the history of every movement that comes out of the barrel - our almanac has all of it. Then cards the moment it scores. Do not miss this one.

title: The Hopper Spoke: Snatch and Toes-to-Bar. Now the Workout Is Up for a Vote.
dek: The original 2007 barrel was spun at Opening Ceremonies this morning and out came two movements: the snatch and the toes-to-bar. The final workout structure is being decided by a vote, and the field races it tonight. Here is the Games history of both movements - and the one man in this field who has already won this exact combination.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: The 2026 hopper draw happened at Opening Ceremonies on Friday morning: the balls that came out of the original 2007 drum were the SNATCH and TOES-TO-BAR, with the final workout structure being decided by a vote before the field contests it in the Friday night session. Our almanac counts 26 Games events featuring a snatch and 12 featuring toes-to-bar. The combination has exactly one precedent: the 2024 Dickies Triplet (runs, toes-to-bars, dumbbell snatches), won by Jayson Hopper - the reigning champion, in this field, sitting 8th. Also in the field: Guilherme Malheiros won the 2021 max snatch (305 lb), Austin Hatfield won 2025 Running Isabel, and Ricky Garard (2022) and Roman Khrennikov (2023) have both won toes-to-bar events. The workout itself is unknown until the vote closes - we update the moment it is official.

blocks.text: The barrel spun this morning, and the sport's oldest randomizer gave Friday night its ingredients: **the snatch and the toes-to-bar**. One barbell movement, one gymnastics movement - the two-modality draw as billed. And there is a twist on top of the twist: **the final workout structure is being decided by a vote** before tonight's session. So the field knows WHAT they will do, but not how much, how heavy, or in what shape. We will publish the workout the moment it is official. Until then, here is what our almanac knows about these two movements - and it knows a lot.
The One Man Who Has Won This Exact Combo

The snatch-plus-toes-to-bar pairing has appeared at the Games exactly once: the **2024 Dickies Triplet** - 5 rounds of a 175-meter run, 12 toes-to-bars and 8 dumbbell snatches, under an 11-minute cap. The men's winner? **Jayson Hopper.** The reigning champion. In this field. Sitting 8th and openly needing a Friday statement. If tonight's vote lands anywhere near a fast triplet shape, the hopper just dealt the champ his favorite hand. (The women's winner of that event, Tia-Clair Toomey, is not in the field - that title is open.)
The Snatch at the Games: 26 Events Deep

The snatch is one of the most-tested movements in Games history - our almanac counts **26 events** featuring it, from the 2009 Max Snatch to the greatest hits: **Amanda** (2010, muscle-ups and squat snatches, won by Chris Spealler and Kristan Clever) and **Isabel** (2012, 30 snatches for time, won by Rich Froning and Annie Thorisdottir). The freshest receipt belongs to this field: **Austin Hatfield won 2025's Running Isabel** (2:35). And the biggest barbell in the building is **Guilherme Malheiros, who won the 2021 max snatch outright at 305 lb**. One more wrinkle: tomorrow's Event 15 is the Speed Snatch Triple - so whatever tonight holds, **the snatchers just got a double-feature weekend**. Malheiros, sitting 20th, suddenly has two events aimed straight at him.
Toes-to-Bar: The Quiet Separator

Twelve Games events have featured toes-to-bars, and they reward a specific, unglamorous skill: rhythm under grip fatigue. The in-field receipts are strong. **Ricky Garard won the 2022 Bike to Work** (a toes-to-bar event) and **Roman Khrennikov won the 2023 Pig Chipper**. On the women's side, **Haley Adams won that same 2022 test** - and toes-to-bar volume has been an Adams signature her whole career. Fraser and Toomey won the 2020 toes-to-bar/lunge event, which tells you what kind of athlete this movement historically rewards: the relentless ones.
What the Vote Decides

Everything, honestly. A heavy barbell turns this into a Malheiros-Mertens event. A light, fast Isabel-style sprint rewards Hatfield, Medeiros and the barbell cyclers. High-volume toes-to-bars bring Adams, Garard and Khrennikov into it. A triplet with running recreates the 2024 event Hopper already won. The beauty of the hopper format is that even after the draw, nobody can prepare - the vote keeps the unknown alive until the last moment. And remember the context: this runs as the FINAL event of a five-event arena day, on tired grip and tired legs.
The moment the vote closes and the workout is official, we publish it with the final picks. Tonight, under the lights, the barrel gets its answer.

title: Event 8: Roman's Answer. Khrennikov Wins the Climbing Snail by Nearly a Minute.
dek: The arena opened and Roman Khrennikov conquered it - a sixth career event win, taken by almost sixty seconds, capped by the first victory interview of his career delivered entirely in English. How the Snail was won, from the broadcast floor.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: Men's Event 8, Climbing Snail 26 (400-lb Snail pushes, legless rope climbs, 30 toes-to-bars, rope climbs, all in a 22-lb vest): Roman Khrennikov won in 5:27.60 per the official results board, 18 seconds clear, ahead of James Sprague (5:46.03) and Dallin Pepper (5:52.12). It is Khrennikov's sixth career Games event win (verified against our almanac: 2020 Row, 2022 Rinse N Repeat and Alpaca, 2023 Pig Chipper and Alpaca Redux). The race story from the broadcast: two strategies emerged in the early heats - Vellner slow on the Snail and fast on the rig, Malheiros the reverse - and Khrennikov simply did both. Sprague passed Hopper mid-event to protect his overall lead. All five fastest times came from the final heat. Overall standings update the moment the official leaderboard posts.

blocks.text: The arena portion of the 2026 Games opened tonight, and the first man to own it was the one Cookeville has been waiting on. **Roman Khrennikov won Event 8, Climbing Snail 26, in 5:27.60** per the official results board - **18 seconds clear of a stacked final heat** (the broadcast's mid-race 'by a minute' call was against earlier-heat pace) - ahead of James Sprague (5:46.03) and Dallin Pepper (5:52.12). It is the **sixth event win of his Games career**, and we checked that number against our almanac: the 2020 1,000m Row, the 2022 Rinse N Repeat and Alpaca, the 2023 Pig Chipper and Alpaca Redux, and now the Snail.
How It Was Won

The early heats produced two competing blueprints. In heat one, Patrick Vellner went **slower on the Snail, faster on the rig and rope**, and won the heat. In heat two, Guilherme Malheiros flipped it - **fast Snail, slower rig** - and won his. Then heat three answered the debate: Khrennikov did both. On the broadcast his rope work drew a coaching clinic of praise - heels tucked under the hips, a locked-down foot clamp, "textbook rope climbing" - and once his hands touched the final Snail push, the race was over. The broadcast put it simply: he might beat the best time by a minute - and against the earlier heats, he did; in his own heat Sprague held the gap to 18 seconds.

Behind him, the overall race sharpened. **Jayson Hopper paced directly off Khrennikov at the rope and could not hold the cycle rate.** James Sprague passed Hopper mid-event and, in the words of the booth, "did everything he could to keep pace" - he did not get the win, but second place keeps him clear of everyone chasing his overall lead. Every one of the five fastest times came from the final heat.
The Interview That Mattered

The moment of the night was not on the rig. Six career event wins means six winner interviews - and this was **the first one Roman Khrennikov has ever done entirely in English**. "It doesn't matter what place I have in competition, you always support me," he told the crowd, before thanking his wife and son. For an athlete whose career has run through years of visa battles and a translator at every podium, that is not a small thing. The broadcast added the line that frames his whole weekend: he was one foot injury away from being a CrossFit Games champion. Tonight he started Day 2, in their words, in a championship way.
What It Shakes Up

Three storylines move. **Mayhem finally has its 2026 statement** - we called their Day 1 the quietest in years, and their franchise athlete just answered with 100 points. **The Crouch slide continues**: he finished outside the event top ten per the broadcast, which likely costs him a spot to Ricky Garard (5th tonight) in the overall. And the champions delivered in a cluster: Sprague 2nd, Pepper 3rd, Hopper 4th, Garard 5th - the men who came into the arena with resumes stacked the front of this event. Full official standings, the movement arrows, and the updated live board land the moment the leaderboard posts - we publish only official numbers there.
The women take the floor on the same course next. Event 9, the 3D Throw, follows. The arena day is rolling.

title: Event 8 Women: The Gazan Masterclass. Fastest at Everything, Break Included.
dek: Alex Gazan won every split of the Climbing Snail, took a rest in the middle of her final push, and still won by thirteen and a half seconds. Behind her: a rope-climb comeback, a podium through road rash, and a rookie heat win built on pure pacing IQ.
author: Ravikant Dewangan
summary: Women's Event 8, Climbing Snail 26: Alex Gazan won in 4:55.22 - the only woman under five minutes - ahead of Paige Rodgers (5:08.73) and Danielle Brandon (5:23.14). Per the broadcast she had the fastest split on every single section (Snail, legless climbs, toes-to-bars, rope climbs) and still paused mid-way through her final push. It is her second event win of these Games (shoulder press + Snail). Rodgers won heat two by making up all her time on the four rope climbs; Brandon reached the podium a day after a bike crash left her with road rash; rookie Rachel Noel won heat one on pacing IQ. Cringle went 6th to defend her overall lead (now 58 points); Campbell's 11th shrank second place to a one-point race with Sturt. blocks.text: If you want to know what a perfect heavy-skill event looks like, watch Alex Gazan's Event 8. **She won the Climbing Snail in 4:55.22 - the only woman under five minutes - by 13.5 seconds.** And here is the part that should scare the rest of the field: per the broadcast splits she was **fastest on every single section** - the opening 400-lb Snail push, the legless rope climbs (nearly 20 seconds faster than anyone), the 30 toes-to-bars, the four rope climbs - and she still had enough margin to **take a rest in the middle of her final Snail push** and win going away. The booth called it a "down the middle wheelhouse home run pitch" for her. She hit it like one.
Her Second Win of the Weekend

That is **two event wins in these Games for Gazan** - the shoulder press on Wednesday, the Snail tonight - and it moves her to 5th overall (425). The interview afterward told you where it comes from. Asked who she is doing this for: "My family means everything to me. My brother's here, my husband, my mom, my uncle." And on her longtime coach Justin Cotler, who has said for years she has champion potential: "He's believed in me since day one. It's taken me a while to catch up... I'll die on this hill - no one cares more than him." A year removed from the injury that took her out of the 2025 Games, the catch-up looks complete.
The Races Behind Her

**Paige Rodgers (2nd, 5:08.73)** won heat two with a surgical back half - per the broadcast she was behind Danielle Brandon off the Snail and level through the legless climbs, then **made up all her time on the four rope climbs**, described as the smoothest rope work of the session. Mayhem athletes went 2nd in both Snail events tonight. **Danielle Brandon (3rd, 5:23.14)** might be the grit story of the day: she crashed on Wednesday's bike event - road rash, run over by the athletes who fell into her, per the broadcast - and answered with a podium in her **eighth individual Games appearance** (verified: the most experienced woman in this field). With the Handstand Sprint still to come tonight - a movement family she has won three straight of - her Friday is far from over.

And spare a thought for heat one, where **rookie Rachel Noel won on pure pacing IQ**: first to the rope, then a deliberate 30-second rest between legless climbs while others rushed - the exact strategy the event demanded. The toughest watch was **Lydia Fish, visibly limping on a foot injured Wednesday**, still fighting through the Snail. Her line to the floor reporter: "This is just part of sport." Respect.
The Board: A One-Point Race for Second

**Aimee Cringle went 6th and her lead GREW to 58 points** (538) - the mark of a leader having the weekend of her life: she surrendered nothing on an event she did not need to win. The drama is behind her: **Lucy Campbell finished 11th, and second place is now a single point - Campbell 480, Sturt 479.** Lawson (5th tonight) climbs to 4th overall; Brandon's podium lifts her into the top 10 at last.
And One Stat We Owe You From Wednesday

The broadcast surfaced a number that deserves its own headline: in Wednesday's Swim Standard, **Lucy Campbell's 10:55 did not just win the women's event - it beat every man in the field too** (men's winner Ty Jenkins swam 11:09, on an identical prescription - we checked the official scores). Per the broadcast, it is only the seventh time in Games history a woman has topped every individual in a gender-neutral test. Whatever this weekend holds for Campbell, that swim belongs to history.
Event 9, the 3D Throw, is next - the first Games throwing test in 14 years. Our physics picks are on record. Cards the moment it is official.

blocks.text: Five events inside SAP Center. Two lead changes. One scoring error, posted and then revised, that never actually moved the lead. And a closing event that asked the man wearing the jersey to answer for it under direct pressure, with no room left to hide. Sprague answered. Here is how Friday actually went, event by event, number by number.
The Day The Jersey Would Not Sit Still

Sprague walked into Friday holding the overall lead. By the time the last bar was dropped Friday night, that lead had changed hands exactly twice, survived one posted-then-revised scoring error, and still ended the day exactly where it started: on him.

The first crack came in Event 9, the 3D Throw - a 50-point event, the first since 2016. Malheiros won it at 123 feet, but the story for the standings was Sprague's final throw. He slipped on it and finished 16th. That was lead change number one: Pepper moved into the overall lead, 543 to 534, the first time in his individual career he had worn the jersey.

Event 10, the Run Hang Squat Clean, handed it back. Sprague ducked under the 15-minute mark late, going 15:00.07 for 6th, while Pepper finished in 15:19.14 for 10th. Lead change number two: Sprague back on top, 614 to 607.

Then came the scare. After Event 11, the Handstand Sprint, officials initially posted Medeiros as the overall leader at 674 points. The number was wrong. The scoring team issued a revision, and officially Sprague never lost the lead - he retained it, 664 points to Medeiros's 648, with Crouch at 644 and Pepper at 642 packed in right behind. In the event itself, the margin between fifth and sixth was a single hundredth of a second - Crouch 5th in 2:05.48, Medeiros 6th in 2:05.49.

Event 12, The Hopper, was the last exam of the day, and Sprague did not need to win it. He needed to survive it. He finished 4th in 5:10.54, behind Mertens, Crouch, and Jayson Hopper, and that was enough. The jersey never left his shoulders.
The Event Winners

Event 8, Climbing Snail 26, belonged to Khrennikov, and he did not make it close. He crossed in 5:27.60 for the 6th win of his career - a resume that already included the 2020 Row, the 2022 RnR and Alpaca, and the 2023 Pig Chipper and Alpaca Redux. Sprague was next across in 5:46.03, Pepper took 3rd in 5:52.12, Hopper was 4th, Garard 5th. The heats told their own tactical story: Vellner won heat 1 going slow on the Snail and fast on the rope, Malheiros won heat 2 doing the exact reverse, and Roman split the difference by doing both. Sprague passed Hopper mid-event on the way to that 2nd place. But the moment of the day belonged to what happened after the clock stopped. Khrennikov gave his first victory interview ever conducted entirely in English. "It doesn't matter what place I have, you always support me," he said, thanking his wife and son after years of visa battles.

Event 9 was Malheiros's, and it fit a pattern. His 123-foot 3D Throw was the 6th win of his career, and one of the previous five was the 2022 Sandbag Ladder - sandbags keep finding this man. His wife and 6-month-old daughter were in the crowd. "It takes the pressure off," he said. "I just go back to what I am." He was not done for the day either, adding a 2nd place finish in Event 11's Handstand Sprint for his second podium of Friday. Behind him in the throw, Vellner and rookie Dylan Hamming tied for 2nd at 122 feet - Hamming delivering exactly what our physics-based pre-Games pick projected for him.

Event 10 was a statement from Crouch. He won the Run Hang Squat Clean in 14:15.05, more than 13 seconds clear of the field, for the 3rd win of his career after the 2025 Grip Trip and this year's Event 1 Hopper. He did it in running shoes, no belt, no grips. At the finish line: "I'll come back for those red shorts and leader's jersey, baby. Let's go." Behind him, Medeiros edged Adler for 2nd by four tenths of a second, 14:28.63 to 14:29.04, going unbroken in round 3 exactly when the leaders started breaking up their reps. Garard had led the event early and unbroken before a no-rep on his final round-3 rep sank his chance. Rookie Hamming's unbroken heat-1 time of 15:03.30 held as the benchmark until the final heat; he finished 7th.

Event 11 was Hoffer's, and it was not close. He won the Handstand Sprint in 1:05.62, roughly 25 seconds ahead of the field, for the first win of his career - zero prior wins on record. He trained French artistic gymnastics from age 3, and our own ring-event research had already flagged his gymnastics background as badly underrated. Rookie Ben Fowler of New Zealand took 3rd in 1:50.18, his first career podium, while Haapalainen finished 4th - and later set the record straight that he is not racing hurt: his Achilles injury was about 20 months ago and he has fully recovered.

Event 12, The Hopper 2026, drawn live from the original 2007 drum at Opening Ceremonies and shaped by fan vote into three rounds of 21 toes-to-bar plus unbroken sets of 7 power snatches, 7 hang snatches, and 7 squat snatches at 95 pounds, went to Mertens in 4:55.57 - his 3rd win of these Games, joining wins in the squat and press events. The strength man closed the day by winning a light-bar discipline test. Crouch was 2nd in 4:59.27, and reigning champion Jayson Hopper took 3rd in 5:08.23 - the winner of the only prior snatch-plus-toes-to-bar combo, the 2024 Dickies Triplet, exactly as our almanac read it.
Who Rose, Who Slid
The day ended: Sprague 752, Crouch 740, Medeiros 732, Pepper 718, Garard 675, Hopper 647, Khrennikov 592, Mertens 559, Adler 520, Hoffer 514.

Crouch is the clearest riser of the day. A win in Event 10 and a 2nd in Event 12 pushed him to 740 and 2nd overall, close enough to feel Sprague's lead breathing on his neck. Medeiros holds 3rd at 732 on the strength of a hard-fought 2nd in Event 10 and a 5th in Event 12; the scoreboard moment that briefly showed him at 674 was a posting error, revised - he never held the lead. Pepper's day was a rise and a slide in the same 24 hours - a first-ever leader jersey after Event 9, then finishes of 10th and 19th in Events 10 and 11 dropped him to 4th overall at 718. Garard's Event 10 no-rep cost him a shot at that event, but a 5th in the Climbing Snail kept him at 675 for 5th overall. Hoffer's Event 11 masterpiece is what pushed him into the top 10 outright at 514, and Khrennikov's Snail win was not enough by itself to lift him higher than 7th at 592.
Saturday

The top four are separated by 34 points with eight events still on the board - five Saturday (Events 13 through 17), three Sunday (Events 18 through 20). Saturday opens with Event 13, the 500-meter sprint. Garard won the 2024 Track and Field event, and he is our pick to be the man to beat again. Event 15, the Speed Snatch Triple, follows later in the day. Nothing about Friday suggests this field is done rearranging itself.

blocks.text: Second place at the CrossFit Games changed hands three times on Friday, the fourth flip of the week. First place did not move once. That is the story of the women's field right now, and it is also not close to the whole story, because five events happened underneath that fortress at the top and every one of them mattered. **Cringle** walked into the day up 58 points, sitting at 538, having not put a foot wrong all week. She walked out of it still in the leader's jersey - and somehow that still was not the headline. The headline was a workout programmed by **Tia Toomey** herself, chosen by fan vote, that ended with Cringle crossing the line nearly even with **Lawson** and her time failing to register on the clock. Officials are still reviewing it.
But start where the day started. Four events - the Climbing Snail, the 3D Throw, Run Hang Squat Clean, and the Handstand Sprint - built the drama before anyone got anywhere near that buzzer.
The Fortress

Cringle's Friday, event by event, reads like a highlight reel for a competitor who does not need to win anything - she just needs to not lose it. Sixth on the Climbing Snail, and her lead grew to 65. A quiet 17th on the 3D Throw, the lone event all week she has finished outside the top 10. Fourth on Run Hang Squat Clean, banking points while the leaderboard beneath her rearranged itself violently. Eighth on the Handstand Sprint, one more clean, exactly-what-a-leader-needs result. Four events, one finish outside the top 10, and the margin kept growing anyway.

Then came Toomey's workout, and for the first time all week there was a moment nobody could score. Cringle came off the finish nearly step for step with Lawson, but her time did not initially register. Officials pulled the redundancies and started reviewing. Her exact placing on the event - and the standings that follow from it - are pending the official board.

What is not pending is what she said walking away from it. 'Not really [what we expected],' she admitted. 'It is nice to just wear it... I was not expecting to be wearing this going into the third day. Just taking everything in and enjoying it.' That humility is doing real work for her right now, because one question got louder on Friday: she faded on the final day last year. Can she hold it now that all eyes are on her? So far she has given the doubters almost nothing - top 10 in everything but that single 17th through eleven events, playing, as the broadcast put it, with house money. Saturday is the day all of that gets tested with every camera in the building pointed at her jersey instead of somebody else's.
The Carousel Beneath Her

If Cringle's day was about standing still at the top, second place spent Friday getting thrown around. **Campbell** started the morning holding it by a single point over **Sturt**, 480 to 479. It did not survive the first two events.
Campbell finished 11th on the Climbing Snail, and by the end of the 3D Throw the totals had flipped: Sturt 511, Campbell 510. Same one-point gap, pointed the other way.

Then Run Hang Squat Clean turned personal. Campbell got a rep ahead late with the finish in sight, looking like she might win the thing outright - then a bobble on her final set of bar work opened a door that should not have been open, and Lawson slipped through it, out-touching her at the line by 1.68 seconds. Lawson's **third career win**, her first since coming back from a back injury. Campbell had to settle for second on the workout. But second on the workout, with Sturt stuck in 10th, was still enough - Campbell leapfrogged straight back into second place overall. One flip lost on the floor, one flip won on the scoreboard, in the same event.

It did not hold either. The Handstand Sprint went to someone else, and while Campbell and Sturt both finished outside the top 10, Lawson - who had started the morning sitting fifth overall - kept climbing. By the time the board updated after Event 11, official, she had gone from fifth to second in a single day, the surge of these Games: Cringle **738**, Lawson **650**, Campbell **639**, Gazan **603**, Sturt **596**. Sturt had held second place as recently as the sandbag throw; by evening she was fifth.
The Gamer's Answer

Nobody's Friday had more turns in it than Campbell's. She opened with an 11th on the Snail that cost her second place overall. She spent Run Hang Squat Clean doing everything right until one bobble handed the workout away at the line. By the time Toomey's finale rolled around, she had every reason to be tight.

Instead she played it like someone who had already decided how it was going to go. Three rounds of 21 toes-to-bar into 7-7-7 unbroken snatches at 65 pounds, six-minute cap - and Campbell built in exactly **one planned break** on the toes-to-bar every single round, then hung onto the bar rather than letting go. The broadcast had her just ahead of Cringle and Lawson when she needed it the most, and she crossed first in **5:02.48** - her **sixth career win** at the Games, joining 2022's Rinse N Repeat and Jackie Pro, 2025's Grip Trip and Hammer Down, and this year's Swim Standard.

What she said after told you more than the strategy did. 'I was insanely nervous coming into this whole week,' Campbell admitted. 'There is a different chat when you come second. And the person who won obviously... not being here this year.' Then, almost as an aside about the workout itself: 'the run up is the absolute worst.' It was not a win that fixes her whole week by itself. But it was exactly the answer a competitor needs after losing one at the line earlier in the day.
The Days of Their Lives

**Gazan** owned the morning. She won the Climbing Snail in 4:55.22 - the only woman under five minutes, fastest on every split per the broadcast, and comfortable enough to take a rest in the middle of her final push and still win by 13.5 seconds. It was her second win of these Games, and she backed it up in the very next event with a third-place sandbag throw of 100 feet. Afterward, the credit went straight to coach Justin Cotler: 'He's believed in me since day one... no one cares more than him.'

**Domit** put together the breakout double of the day. First, a maiden Games win on the 3D Throw - launching the sandbag 108 feet in the 50-point event by throwing it 'like a snatch... power from the hips' while others 'kettlebell-swung' it. Her line afterward said everything about where her head was: 'I do wish this event was 100 points, but it's not too late to change that, right?' Then, in the day's finale, she came back and took second on Toomey's Hopper, 5:04.36, edging Danielle Brandon in their heat by 0.57 seconds on her speed between stations. Two different skills, same day, same competitor breaking out exactly when it mattered. (**Hannah Black**, who had shut down her rope climbs on the Snail to protect the rest of her weekend, finished right behind Domit at 106 feet - our physics pick as the heaviest woman in the field, by 7 kilograms, finally cashing in.)

**Rodgers** had her own double. Second on the Climbing Snail, where she made up all of her lost time on the rope climbs, then back out later in the day to win the Handstand Sprint outright in 1:56.58 - her **first career Games win**, on the same day as her runner-up finish. Fuliano took second in the sprint at 2:03.55.

Earlier in the day, limping through the Snail on the foot that has bothered her for two days, **Lydia Fish** put it plainly: 'this is just part of sport.' Hours later, on an event spent almost entirely upside down, that foot stopped mattering - third place on the Handstand Sprint, 2:36.49, a Games podium built on an ankle that had no business allowing one. She was not up there alone, either: two more athletes managing injured ankles, Raptis and Greer, took fourth and fifth right behind her.

And then there was **Danielle Brandon**, whose Friday ran the full range. In the morning she took third on the Climbing Snail, 5:23.14, a day after a bike crash left her with road rash. Then she came into the Handstand Sprint as the winner of three straight handstand-family events from 2021 through 2023 - and finished outside the top 10 in the one discipline she had owned for years. Ninety minutes later, on Toomey's Hopper, she answered: third place, 5:04.93, a podium on the same afternoon her streak died. Not everyone gets a chance to respond to a bad result before the day is even over. Brandon took hers.
Saturday

The pressure at the top of this leaderboard has changed shape. It stopped being about closing a gap - Cringle's cushion stood at 88 points over second place after 11 events - and became about whether she can hold the jersey with the whole broadcast, and the whole field, watching to see if she fades on the final day the way she did last year. The one loose thread is not even her doing: a finish that did not register on Toomey's workout, still pending the official board. Otherwise Friday gave them nothing to point to but a leader banking top-10s so quietly it made an 88-point lead feel routine.

Everything else is still moving underneath her. Lawson brings more momentum than anyone after climbing from fifth to second on the official Event 11 board. Campbell arrives having just beaten Toomey's own workout with her nerves showing and a sixth career win in hand. Sturt, second by a single point as recently as the sandbag throw, starts Saturday from fifth on that same Event 11 board. Cringle's placing on Event 12, and the overall standings that follow from it, are not official yet - that comes with the review. What is official is this: the leader has not blinked through two full days, and Saturday is the day everyone finds out if that holds when it counts the most.
Update: The Buzzer Verdict (added overnight)

The official review settled it, and the ending is better than fiction. **Cringle was credited 4th on the hopper at 5:05** - the leader, under all that pressure, delivering a top-4 on the final event of the day. And the ripple decided the silver race: her credited time moved **Lawson to 5th on the event, which handed second place overall back to Campbell by five points - 739 to 734.** Second place changed hands FOUR times on Friday alone: Sturt took it after the throw, Campbell took it back on the run event, Lawson seized it on the handstands, and Campbell reclaimed it by winning Toomey's hopper. The official end-of-Day-2 board: **Cringle 826 (an 87-point lead), Campbell 739, Lawson 734, Sturt 652, Gazan 636.** The fortress holds. The gamer is back in second. And Saturday now has everything to shoot at.

dek: Second place changed hands three times on Friday. First place never moved. Then Tia Toomey's own workout ended with the leader's time stuck in review.
summary: Cringle's lead never blinked through Friday's five events, ending with her Hopper time under official review, while second place flipped three times behind her - Sturt by a point, Campbell answering, Lawson surging from fifth - and Campbell won Tia Toomey's fan-voted Hopper for her sixth career win, hours after losing Run Hang Squat Clean at the line.
